content.headline: Israel votes as Hebron operation displaces families and Netanyahu seeks a newerm
content.shortHeadline: Israel votes amid a Hebron crackdown
content.standfirst: Voters choose a parliament amid a close contest over Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership. In Hebron, Palestinians say military restrictions and forced evacuations have left families unsure when—or whether—they can return home.

image.caption: A screen in Tel Aviv shows Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot ahead of the election.

sources.originalTitle: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
ANALYSE: Et såret og hærdet Israel går til valg
Et dødeligt angreb har ført til nedlukning for en kvart million mennesker: ‘Det er kollektiv afstraffelse’

segments.title: A close contest
segments.body: Israel’s first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 is a test of Benjamin Netanyahu’s record and the country’s political direction. Polls suggest his coalition could lose its majority, but the opposition is divided and may struggle to form a government.

perspectives.body: DR’s analysis argues that, whatever the election result, Israeli society has shifted to the right and a change of government alone is unlikely to reverse that change.

segments.title: Hebron under restrictions
segments.body: After two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a Hebron checkpoint, Israel’s military sealed routes into and out of the city and ordered some residents from their homes. A Palestinian official says about 1,200 people were displaced. Israel says its operation is aimed at finding militants and weapons; Hebron’s mayor calls the measures collective punishment.

content.headline: Ukraine truce begins to allow aid and evacuations in occupied Oleshky
content.shortHeadline: Truce begins in occupied Ukrainian city
content.standfirst: A ceasefire is intended to let aid reach Oleshky and allow civilians to leave. Ukraine says it is observing the agreement, but its duration, monitoring arrangements and the details of the humanitarian operation remain unclear.

sources.originalTitle: Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump
Rusland: Våbenhvile er trådt i kraft i Olesjky i det sydlige Ukraine

segments.body: A truce has begun in Russian-occupied Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from Kherson, to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. Russia says it stopped firing in the area at 04:00 Moscow time; Ukraine’s human rights commissioner says Ukraine is honouring its commitments.

perspectives.body: DR reports that AFP could not verify whether attacks had decreased after the truce began. Its account gives a lower estimate of the remaining population—about 2,000 people, including 50 children—than the BBC’s estimate of 6,000 people and 200 children.

segments.title: What remains uncertain
segments.body: The city has been under Russian occupation since 2022, and residents have faced shortages of food and medicine. Neither side has said how long the ceasefire will last or who will monitor it; details of the planned aid and evacuation operation have not been provided.

content.headline: Lula’s victory sets up a new test of Brazil’s relationship with Trump
content.shortHeadline: Lula’s win tests ties with Trump’s US
content.standfirst: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s fourth-term victory defied the regional rightward trend and drew an unsupported claim of election fraud from Donald Trump. The immediate political fallout includes a court order against defeated candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

image.caption: Lula and running mate Geraldo Alckmin address supporters after Lula won the presidential runoff in São Paulo.

sources.originalTitle: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
Lederen af Bolsonaros parti anerkender brasiliansk valgnederlag
Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports

segments.title: A win with international consequences
segments.body: Lula won 51.79% of the vote after trailing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round, becoming the first Brazilian president since the return to civilian rule to win after finishing second initially. Trump called the election “rigged” without offering evidence, even as he said he liked Lula and got along with him.

segments.title: Tensions—and a court order
segments.body: The relationship between Lula and Trump has thawed since a dispute over US tariffs, but disagreements over US military action in the region, Brazil’s payment system Pix and American influence could bring tensions back. Separately, a Brazilian Supreme Court justice ordered Flávio Bolsonaro to surrender his passports and barred him from leaving the country, citing an ongoing police investigation.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that the passport order also prohibits Bolsonaro from contacting a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were used to launder money. Bolsonaro denies saying he would leave Brazil if he lost the election.

content.headline: Jordan strikes armed groups in Syria after church attack; civilians reportedlyk
content.shortHeadline: Jordan strikes armed groups in Syria
content.standfirst: Jordan says its air force targeted armed groups after a church attack killed nine people in Karak. Syrian officials say five civilians, including women and children, died in the strikes; the two governments gave differing accounts of coordination.

image.caption: Syrian officials say five people were killed in a Jordanian strike on a village in Daraa province.

sources.originalTitle: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack
Jordan carries out deadly strike in Syria in retaliation for church attack

segments.body: Jordan says it carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, Jordan, which killed nine people. Syrian officials say five civilians were killed in a strike in Daraa province. Jordan says the operation was coordinated with Damascus; Syria says it was not notified and has opened an investigation.

segments.title: Border crossing closed
segments.body: Syria closed the Nassib crossing, the only passenger and commercial border crossing between the two countries, suspending traffic in both directions. Jordanian authorities arrested three men over the church attack; their motive remains unknown, and no group has claimed responsibility.

content.headline: James Comey faces new federal charges as judge orders daughter’s reinstatement
content.shortHeadline: Comey faces new charges; daughter wins reinstatement
content.standfirst: Prosecutors have filed two charges against former FBI director James Comey over an alleged disclosure of national defence information. Separately, a judge ruled his daughter was illegally fired as a federal prosecutor and ordered her reinstated with back pay.

image.caption: Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor, was ordered reinstated with back pay.

sources.originalTitle: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules

segments.title: New charges against James Comey
segments.body: The charges concern an alleged 2016 disclosure to The New York Times, according to Comey’s lawyers. Comey denies wrongdoing and calls the case an abuse of the justice department. His lawyers have asked for the charges to be dismissed; one former prosecutor cited by the BBC says a 10-year statute of limitations could be an obstacle.

segments.title: A separate ruling involving his daughter
segments.body: A federal judge ruled that Maurene Comey was illegally fired from her job as a prosecutor in New York and ordered the government to reinstate her and provide back pay. The Justice Department disagrees with the ruling and says it will appeal.

content.headline: Anthropic warns of catastrophic AI risks in US stock listing filing
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic flags AI risks ahead of US listing
content.standfirst: The Claude developer’s filing for a planned Nasdaq listing warns that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks if misused or deployed without safeguards. The company also disclosed substantial losses, major infrastructure dependencies and uncertain listing details.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing

segments.title: A landmark listing—and a warning
segments.body: Anthropic says it plans to list on Nasdaq, but has not yet disclosed the share price range, number of shares or date. Its filing warns that advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” without appropriate safeguards. The company reported $16.3bn in revenue and losses of more than $80.7bn in the first half of 2026.

segments.title: Risks for the company
segments.body: The filing also cites reliance on cloud providers, Taiwanese chipmakers and data centres concentrated in the US, as well as possible regulatory action over harms associated with its models. The company presents AI as a potentially transformative technology, while saying its business depends on developing advanced models and managing the risks they create.

content.headline: India’s Jio listing could signal an end to years of cheap mobile data
content.shortHeadline: Jio listing may mean pricier mobile data
content.standfirst: Jio’s planned $3.2bn share sale is drawing strong investor demand, but analysts say pressure to deliver returns could weaken its incentive to keep tariffs low for more than 550 million subscribers.

image.caption: Jio’s discounted data plans have helped make mobile internet widely accessible in India.

sources.originalTitle: India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions

segments.title: A landmark share sale
segments.body: Jio Platforms, owned by Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is due to make its stock-market debut on Wednesday in what the BBC describes as India’s largest-ever initial public offering. The company has about 553 million mobile subscribers and carries a large share of the country’s wireless data traffic.

segments.title: What it could mean for customers
segments.body: Analysts say a listed Jio may focus more on revenue per subscriber than on gaining customers through very low prices. That could bring higher bills for users and make it easier for competitors to raise their tariffs too. The extent and timing of any price changes remain uncertain.

content.headline: Pope Leo’s South American tour to go ahead after lung cancer surgery
content.shortHeadline: Pope’s South American tour to proceed after surgery
content.standfirst: The Vatican says Pope Leo will keep his November travel plans after surgery to remove a localised tumour from his right lung. He is recovering and adjusting his schedule in consultation with his doctors.

sources.originalTitle: Pope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery

segments.body: Pope Leo is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November, travelling to 10 cities. The Vatican says tests showed the cancer was localised and that there are no clinical reasons to cancel the trip. The 71-year-old had surgery on 13 October and was discharged from hospital four days later.

segments.title: Recovery and itinerary
segments.body: The Pope has been resting and gradually resuming his duties, with his daily schedule adjusted in consultation with doctors. The Vatican says he is looking forward to returning to South America, where he spent years as a missionary and later worked between Peru and the United States.

content.headline: Budget will replace carer’s allowance cliff edge with tapered payments
content.shortHeadline: Carer’s allowance to be tapered, ending cliff-edge rule
content.standfirst: The planned change would remove £1 of allowance for each extra £1 earned above the weekly limit, instead of withdrawing a full week’s payment. It follows years of debts and penalties for carers who exceeded the threshold by small amounts.

image.caption: The planned taper would remove £1 of carer’s allowance for each additional £1 earned above the limit.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Unfair’ cliff-edge rule that punished carers to be abolished in budget

segments.title: A change to the earnings rule
segments.body: The chancellor, John Healey, is expected to announce a digital taper for carer’s allowance in Wednesday’s Budget. Under the proposed system, £1 of benefit would be removed for each £1 earned above the £204 weekly limit, replacing a rule that can remove the full £86.45 weekly payment if earnings exceed the limit by even a penny.

segments.title: Debts and delayed reform
segments.body: A review found that about 180,000 carers built up overpayment debts totalling £300m between 2019 and 2025. Campaigners welcomed the planned change but say a new digital system is not expected before the end of the decade. The Budget is also expected to include other measures, but wider proposals remain unconfirmed.

content.headline: UK shop price inflation rises to its highest level in two and a half years
content.shortHeadline: UK shop price inflation hits two-and-a-half-year high
content.standfirst: The British Retail Consortium says shop prices rose 2.1% year on year in October, up from 1.4% in September, as retailers pass on some higher costs. Food inflation also increased, adding pressure ahead of Wednesday’s Budget.

image.caption: The BRC says food and non-food prices both rose in October.

sources.originalTitle: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises

segments.title: Prices rise
segments.body: The British Retail Consortium says shop price inflation reached 2.1% in October, its highest level in two and a half years. Food inflation rose to 2.9% from 2.5%, while non-food inflation more than doubled to 1.7%. The group says retailers have absorbed higher costs for two years but are now starting to pass them on.

segments.title: Pressure on household budgets
segments.body: The report links rising costs for energy and food ingredients to the conflict in the Middle East. A separate study cited by the Guardian found low-income families were changing what they buy, using reduced-price sections and sometimes leaving the heating off. The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates next week, but further increases are not certain.

content.headline: Report says AI is embedded across Home Office immigration work
content.shortHeadline: Report raises concerns over Home Office use of AI
content.standfirst: Open Rights Group says AI is used in areas including asylum casework and border surveillance, warning that limited transparency risks bias and discrimination. The Home Office says the tools assist staff and do not make asylum decisions.

image.caption: The report says AI is used in areas including border surveillance and asylum casework.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Digital hostile environment’: AI secretly being embedded across Home Office, report claims

segments.title: Uses and concerns
segments.body: Open Rights Group says AI is involved in work ranging from summarising asylum interviews to surveillance and prioritising immigration cases. Its report draws on published material, freedom of information requests and parliamentary questions, and argues that secrecy makes it difficult to assess the systems’ accuracy, safeguards and effects on people seeking protection.

segments.title: The Home Office response
segments.body: The Home Office says AI is only one tool used to protect the border and does not replace human decision-makers. It says trained caseworkers make asylum decisions, AI tools assist with navigating interview records and policy information, and the department monitors their performance and plans to publish updated evaluations.

content.headline: Russell Brand’s former assistant tells court his behaviour was normalised
content.shortHeadline: Former assistant gives evidence at Russell Brand trial
content.standfirst: Helen Berger told Southwark Crown Court she saw Brand treat women poorly and was asked to obtain women’s phone numbers. Brand denies charges of rape and sexual assault; Berger said she never witnessed him doing anything unlawful.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial told

segments.body: Helen Berger, who worked as Russell Brand’s assistant from 2006 to 2007, told the court that people around him normalised and dismissed his behaviour. She alleged that he had an “insane sexual appetite” and that he asked her to get female fans’ phone numbers. She said she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.

segments.title: The charges
segments.body: Brand faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault relating to six women and allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges. Berger said she did not witness him doing anything against the law, but said she saw him treat women poorly.

content.headline: Former rough sleepers describe what helped them off the streets
content.shortHeadline: Former rough sleepers say local support is vital
content.standfirst: As Andy Burnham promises £432m to sustain support for people sleeping rough, people with experience of homelessness describe the services that helped them—and the gaps that left them without help.

image.caption: Martin Fletcher outside the building used by Basis Sunderland before the housing charity closed.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Local services are vital’: Former rough sleepers on what helped them off the streets

segments.title: What helped people find housing
segments.body: People interviewed by the Guardian describe different routes off the streets: a charity worker who listened without overwhelming them with forms, a hostel place that made it possible to reconnect with treatment services, and supported accommodation after prison. One Sunderland charity that helped a former rough sleeper has since closed for lack of funding.

segments.title: Challenges for the government’s plan
segments.body: Burnham told a Downing Street summit that a further £432m would sustain support into next year. People with experience of homelessness warn that services can be hard to access, hostel placements can fail people with addiction, and practical help is needed for people without phones. A former prisoner said he was given no accommodation when released.

content.headline: More wind warnings follow two UK storm deaths and widespread power cuts
content.shortHeadline: New wind warnings as storm recovery continues
content.standfirst: Two people were killed by falling trees and hundreds of thousands of properties lost power during Storm Boelo and Storm Austen. Further warnings cover parts of the UK on Monday and Tuesday, with the strongest gusts forecast in northern Scotland.

image.caption: Waves hit the sea wall at New Brighton during Storm Boelo on Sunday.

sources.originalTitle: The areas facing new weather warnings over 70mph winds – and when they’ll end

segments.title: Deaths and disruption
segments.body: Two men were killed by falling trees on Sunday, and two women were taken to hospital after another tree struck them in Scotland. The Energy Networks Association said 39,000 customers were still without power at 8am on Monday; 13 primary schools in Aberdeenshire were also closed because of outages.

segments.title: More severe weather forecast
segments.body: The Met Office issued further yellow wind warnings for Monday and Tuesday, with gusts of more than 70mph possible in parts of northern and north-western Scotland. Flood warnings and alerts were also in force. The forecaster expects conditions to become quieter and drier for much of the UK from Wednesday.

content.headline: UK to launch independent review into Henry Nowak’s death in police custody
content.shortHeadline: Independent review announced into teenager’s death
content.standfirst: The review will examine the events before and after 18-year-old Henry Nowak was fatally stabbed and died while in police custody. It will begin its second phase after a separate investigation into officers’ actions is complete.

image.caption: The case prompted scrutiny of police handling of the stabbing and Henry Nowak’s death.

sources.originalTitle: Britisk drabssag vakte opsigt: Nu skal den undersøges

segments.body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the death of Henry Nowak, who was 18 when he was stabbed last year. A body-camera video that emerged in June showed officers handcuffing him and not responding when he asked for help, according to DR’s report.

segments.title: Scope and next steps
segments.body: The review will examine what authorities knew about the man convicted of Nowak’s murder, and whether opportunities to intervene were missed. It will cover police, health services, local authorities and education institutions. A second phase will follow the Independent Office for Police Conduct investigation into officers at the scene; a report is expected in about five months.

content.headline: Danish radar company wins record 625m-kroner order for Poland’s anti-drone def
content.shortHeadline: Weibel wins record order for Poland’s anti-drone system
content.standfirst: Allerød-based Weibel Scientific will supply radar for Poland’s planned drone defence network, in a 625m-kroner contract the company calls its largest order. The deal also places it in a wider European effort to detect and counter drones.

sources.originalTitle: Hybridkrig og droner får Polen til at købe dansk isenkram for 625 millioner kroner i Nordsjælland

segments.title: A major export contract
segments.body: Poland’s defence forces have ordered an unspecified number of Xenta radars from Weibel Scientific for 625 million kroner. The company says the contract is the largest in its history. The radars are designed to detect and identify drones and are intended for Poland’s planned system along its borders, including those with Russia’s Kaliningrad region, Belarus and Ukraine.

segments.title: Part of a wider defence push
segments.body: The order could lead to further contracts as other countries develop drone defences and the EU works towards a connected system of sensors and weapons. Lithuania’s national security adviser describes the threat from drones as a major concern along NATO and the EU’s eastern flank. Weibel’s chief executive says the company is expanding production and hiring.

content.headline: Rigshospitalet launches review of treatments after dispute over dismisseddoctors
content.shortHeadline: Rigshospitalet treatments to be reviewed after doctors’ dispute
content.standfirst: A regional politician says an external review will examine earlier treatment cases at the hospital’s transplant and digestive-disease department. The doctors’ association says the information is new and was not part of the dismissals; staff have raised patient-safety concerns.

image.caption: Three senior doctors are leaving Rigshospitalet’s specialised transplant and digestive-disease department.

sources.originalTitle: Balladen om fyringer på Rigshospitalet fortsætter: 'Det her er fuldstændig nye oplysninger'
Efter krisemøde: Regionsrådsformand har tillid til Rigshospitalets ledelse

segments.title: External review announced
segments.body: After a crisis meeting, Region Hovedstaden said an external review would examine previous treatments at Rigshospitalet’s specialised department, including whether procedures for recording experimental surgery were followed. The region’s health committee chair said the hospital had reported experimental surgery without patient consent or documentation; the precise scope of the review remains to be clarified.

segments.title: Staffing and competing accounts
segments.body: Three critical senior doctors are leaving the department, which performs Denmark’s liver transplants. The hospital says the dismissals were necessary and patients can be treated with help from partner hospitals if needed. Twenty-seven operating-room nurses have warned that staffing changes could put patient safety at risk.

perspectives.body: The head of the senior doctors’ association said the information about earlier treatments was entirely new and had not been raised in connection with the dismissals. He said he hoped the hospital was not seeking additional reasons to dismiss the doctors.

content.headline: Danish party promises one pensioner extra 1,000 kroner as wider scheme remains
content.shortHeadline: One pensioner promised extra money as others await details
content.standfirst: The Social Democrats say a pensioner featured in the party’s campaign will receive 1,000 kroner more a month under a proposed benefit for 150,000 people. The final eligibility rules are still being negotiated, and other pensioners do not yet know who will qualify.

image.caption: Mette Frederiksen shared images of a shopping trip with pensioner Annemarie.

sources.originalTitle: 0,000091 procent af landets pensionister har fået løfte om 1.000 kroner ekstra om måneden

segments.title: One named recipient, wider scheme undecided
segments.body: The Social Democrats have promised that Annemarie, a pensioner who appeared in campaign material with Mette Frederiksen, will receive an extra 1,000 kroner a month. The party says about 150,000 pensioners with the lowest incomes are intended to benefit, but the final eligibility model is still under discussion with other parties.

segments.title: Rules remain unsettled
segments.body: A professor of administrative law told DR that politicians may give an individual a particular assurance while a proposal is still being negotiated; once a law is passed, equality rules would apply when detailed regulations are set. The government has not yet specified the cutoff for the wider group.

content.headline: Social Democrats propose state funding to keep some rural schools and care homes
content.shortHeadline: Social Democrats propose help for threatened rural services
content.standfirst: The party wants the state to help fund schools, care homes and community halls at risk of closure because of local government finances, but has not costed the plan. Coalition partners say any support needs limits and further discussion.

image.caption: Social Democrat Bjørn Brandenborg has proposed state support for some local services at risk of closure.

sources.originalTitle: S vil 'udstikke en garanti' til lukningstruede skoler og plejehjem: Ved ikke, hvad det kommer til at koste

segments.title: An uncosted proposal
segments.body: Social Democrat Bjørn Brandenborg says the state should help keep valued local schools, care homes and halls open when councils cannot afford them. He could not say what the proposal would cost. The plan is the Social Democrats’ own and has not been agreed with the other governing parties.

segments.title: Coalition partners seek conditions
segments.body: The Radicals say they will not offer a blank cheque and want clear limits; the Moderates warn against excessive central control of local budgets and suggest support for independent schools instead. The Socialist People’s Party supports the general aim but says the details and cost still need discussion.

content.headline: Conservative majority sends disputed LGBTQ+ healthcare handbook back for rewrite
content.shortHeadline: Region sends LGBTQ+ healthcare handbook back for rewrite
content.standfirst: A majority in Region Syddanmark voted to draw up a new version of guidance for healthcare workers, after a dispute over language and gender. Supporters say the handbook helps staff meet patients’ needs; critics argue it imposes particular terminology.

image.caption: Social Democrat Mette With Hagensen spoke against changing the healthcare handbook.

sources.originalTitle: 'Jeg skal lige sluge det menneskesyn': Håndbog sendt tilbage efter hård debat

segments.title: A divided regional council
segments.body: A conservative majority in Region Syddanmark voted to return a disputed LGBTQ+ handbook for a new draft. The guidance is intended to help healthcare staff communicate with LGBTQ+ patients, including by using gender-neutral pronouns. The change followed an earlier vote against the first draft by a majority on the region’s executive committee.

segments.title: Disagreement over the guidance
segments.body: Venstre’s Pernelle Jensen said the handbook forces staff to use particular terminology. Social Democrat Mette With Hagensen argued that the healthcare system should make room for difference and respond to patients’ needs. A trans man involved in drafting the handbook asked the council what scientific basis supported the view that there are only two genders.

content.headline: Riders raise safety concerns over proposed Danish nature park in Bidstrup
content.shortHeadline: Riders challenge plans for free-roaming horses in new nature park
content.standfirst: Riders say free-roaming horses could make parts of Bidstrup Forest unsafe and restrict access. Lejre’s mayor says the plans have already changed after consultation; the council is due to approve a response before the proposal proceeds.

image.caption: Ane Kirstine Ilsøe rides in Bidstrup Forest, part of the area proposed for a new nature park.

sources.originalTitle: Kritik af ny naturnationalpark: Rytter frygter at blive overfaldet af en hingst i brunst

segments.title: Concerns over access and safety
segments.body: Ane Kirstine Ilsøe and a representative of the Danish Riding Association object to plans for free-roaming horses and cattle in a proposed nature park in Bidstrup Forest. They fear encounters with horses could endanger riders and children and make it harder to use the forest. The park’s stated aim is to strengthen biodiversity.

segments.title: The municipality’s response
segments.body: Lejre’s mayor says the project has changed after a local working group heard from interested parties, including changes to the proposed fencing. The municipal council is due to approve a consultation response for consideration by the Danish Nature Agency and environment ministry.

content.headline: Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for a men’s Ballon d’Or winner
content.shortHeadline: Kane ends England’s 25-year Ballon d’Or wait
content.standfirst: The Bayern Munich striker is the first Englishman to win the men’s award since Michael Owen in 2001, after a season of extraordinary scoring numbers despite missing out on football’s biggest team trophies.

image.caption: Harry Kane broke Bayern Munich’s goalscoring record for a season.

sources.originalTitle: Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend

segments.body: Harry Kane has won the men’s Ballon d’Or, becoming the first English player to receive the award since Michael Owen in 2001. Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe was second and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal third.

segments.title: A record-breaking season
segments.body: Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches for Bayern last season, including 36 in the Bundesliga and 14 in the Champions League. His total across club and England matches was 73 goals in 65 games, even though Bayern lost in the Champions League semi-finals and England fell short at the World Cup.

content.headline: Alexia Putellas wins a record-equalling third women’s Ballon d’Or
content.shortHeadline: Putellas claims a record-equalling third Ballon d’Or
content.standfirst: The Spain midfielder returns to the top of the game after injury and a trophy-laden final season at Barcelona. She joined London City Lionesses in July and has already made an impact in the WSL.

image.caption: Alexia Putellas won four trophies with Barcelona last season.

sources.originalTitle: Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or

segments.body: Alexia Putellas has won the women’s Ballon d’Or for a third time, matching Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati’s tally. Her award keeps the honour in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year. Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor finished second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.

segments.title: A return to the top
segments.body: Putellas scored 21 goals and made 13 assists in all competitions as Barcelona won four trophies in 2025-26. After a career-threatening ACL injury in 2022 and a gradual return to form, she took on a leading creative role before leaving her childhood club for London City Lionesses. She has three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new side.

content.headline: Carrick’s future in doubt as Manchester United consider potential successors
content.shortHeadline: Carrick’s future in doubt at Manchester United
content.standfirst: Michael Carrick has left United’s training ground after talks about his position, with the club’s winless run placing him under major pressure. Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are among the names being considered if he goes.

image.caption: Manchester United have gone eight matches without a victory under Michael Carrick.

sources.originalTitle: Howe and Nagelsmann high on Man Utd's list if Carrick sacked
Why is Wilcox in line of fire from Man Utd fans?

segments.body: Carrick’s position is under serious threat after Manchester United went eight matches without a win. He left the club’s training ground on Monday after talks over his future, but no decision on his role is confirmed. BBC Sport reports that work to identify possible successors is under way.

segments.title: Scrutiny reaches beyond the manager
segments.body: Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are prominent among the candidates United have explored, and both are said to know of the club’s interest. Meanwhile, fans have also turned on director of football Jason Wilcox after the Bournemouth defeat.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport’s account of the scrutiny around Wilcox notes that he does not control United’s transfer budgets. It also says the club has not explained why it focused on midfield in the summer rather than adding cover at left-back and up front.

content.headline: Lancashire to consider farewell for James Anderson after members’ anger
content.shortHeadline: Lancashire considers an Anderson farewell
content.standfirst: Members challenged Lancashire over releasing the England great, prompting the club to look into a farewell. Anderson has not announced his retirement, and other counties are interested in signing him.

image.caption: James Anderson has taken more wickets than any other pace bowler in Test cricket.

sources.originalTitle: Lancashire consider Anderson farewell amid fan unrest

segments.body: Lancashire will look into arranging a farewell for James Anderson after the decision not to renew his contract prompted anger at a members’ meeting. Some members said the end-of-season announcement denied fans the chance to thank the bowler for his service; the club agreed to consider a solution.

segments.title: A question still open
segments.body: Anderson took 50 wickets last season and was named Lancashire’s Championship player of the year. The club says it wants to build a squad to win the County Championship within four years and does not expect the 44-year-old to be part of that plan. Anderson has expressed sadness at the release but has stopped short of retiring; several counties are interested in speaking with him.

content.headline: England’s Under-15 World Cup match with Republic of Ireland abandoned after a ‘[
content.shortHeadline: England-Ireland U15 match abandoned after racism allegation
content.standfirst: England left the pitch after a player reported an alleged racist comment during their World Cup match in Azerbaijan. The Republic of Ireland were leading 4-1; Fifa says it is gathering reports and will refer the matter for disciplinary consideration.

image.caption: England players gathered at the side of the pitch after the alleged incident.

sources.originalTitle: England-Republic of Ireland U15 World Cup game ends over alleged racism

segments.body: England’s Under-15 team walked off during their Group C match against the Republic of Ireland after alleging that an opposition player had used a racist slur. The referee abandoned the game with Ireland leading 4-1. The allegation has not been established.

segments.title: Investigation underway
segments.body: Fifa said it was gathering official reports and that the matter would be referred to its independent disciplinary committee, which will decide in due course. The Football Association said it was awaiting more information and was in contact with Fifa; it described the players’ wellbeing as a priority.

content.headline: Doubles players urge ATP to rethink proposed draw and prize-money cuts
content.shortHeadline: Doubles players fight proposed ATP cuts
content.standfirst: More than 150 men’s doubles players, along with former players and national federations, have signed a letter opposing changes proposed for 2028. The ATP says its review aims to strengthen the tour; a board vote is due next month.

image.caption: Henry Patten and Harri Heliovaara, reigning Wimbledon champions, signed the open letter.

sources.originalTitle: Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cuts

segments.body: The players’ open letter urges the ATP not to halve doubles draws at its leading Masters 1000 events and smaller tournaments, or reduce doubles’ share of prize money from 20% to 10%. The signatories argue the proposals could damage careers and the future of the discipline.

segments.title: A decision ahead
segments.body: The ATP says the wider review is intended to create a more sustainable long-term model and that it wants to maintain doubles’ role. It says the proposals are based on analysis of costs, revenue and viewership. The tour’s board is due to vote at next month’s ATP Finals; BBC Sport reports that ATP sources expect a compromise, though players say they see little appetite for negotiation.

content.headline: Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong cited over alleged groin grab
content.shortHeadline: Furlong cited over alleged groin grab
content.standfirst: The Ireland international faces a disciplinary process over an alleged offence during Leinster’s win over Munster. The outcome is not yet known, and a finding against him could put November’s international matches at risk.

image.caption: Tadhg Furlong has been included in Ireland’s squad for November’s Nations Championship fixtures.

sources.originalTitle: Ireland prop Furlong cited over alleged groin grab

segments.body: Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited over an alleged groin grab during Leinster’s 24-18 win over Munster. Munster’s Gavin Coombes raised an allegation about an unnamed Leinster player during the match, but the television match official could not find video evidence at the time. Furlong has since been cited under the relevant foul-play law.

segments.title: Disciplinary process pending
segments.body: The United Rugby Championship says arrangements for the process are under way and will be announced in due course. If found guilty, Furlong could miss Ireland’s Nations Championship matches against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa, as well as club fixtures. Munster coach Clayton McMillan said he would back his players when they make an allegation; Leinster coach Leo Cullen said he had not seen the incident and called it a serious matter.

content.headline: Graeme McDowell confirms he will not pursue LIV Golf’s 2027 reboot
content.shortHeadline: McDowell exits LIV Golf ahead of proposed 2027 reboot
content.standfirst: The former US Open champion is the latest major winner to step away from LIV as it tries to secure players and financing for a new version of the league. Whether LIV 2.0 can proceed remains unresolved.

image.caption: Graeme McDowell joined LIV Golf when the breakaway tour launched in 2022.

sources.originalTitle: Former US Open winner McDowell confirms LIV exit

segments.body: Northern Ireland’s Graeme McDowell has confirmed he will not pursue LIV 2.0, the proposed version of the breakaway tour planned for 2027. The 2010 US Open winner joined LIV at its launch in 2022 and said he was grateful for the past four years and looked forward to the next chapter of his career.

segments.title: The league’s future remains uncertain
segments.body: Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while other players have left or announced plans to do so. LIV’s Saudi backer withdrew its support in April, and the league filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month. It has secured a possible $300m in financing, but a lawyer told a bankruptcy court that the league needs enough players to proceed; whether it will do so is still unclear.

content.headline: Dónal Lunny, a defining figure in Irish music, dies aged 79
content.shortHeadline: Irish music great Dónal Lunny dies aged 79
content.standfirst: The multi-instrumentalist and producer helped shape groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts, and was widely credited with bringing the bouzouki into Irish music.

image.caption: Dónal Lunny performing at the Manchester Apollo in 1999.

sources.originalTitle: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79

segments.body: Dónal Lunny, the Irish traditional musician and producer, has died aged 79 from cancer. A founding member of Planxty, he also played with the Bothy Band, Moving Hearts and Coolfin, and produced 17 albums through his label, Mulligan Records.

segments.title: A lasting musical legacy
segments.body: Ireland’s president, Catherine Connolly, called Lunny central to many of the most influential moments in Irish music over six decades. She highlighted his partnerships with Christy Moore and Andy Irvine, his work as a producer and the recognition he received from fellow artists, including a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish Folk Awards.

content.headline: Jimmy Webb revisits the songs he wrote for Dolly Parton, Glen Campbell and Frank
content.shortHeadline: Jimmy Webb brings his lost songs back to life
content.standfirst: The 80-year-old songwriter discusses a new album of previously unheard material, the performers who made his classics endure and the friendships and losses behind his long career.

image.caption: Jimmy Webb in 1971.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and Frank

segments.body: Jimmy Webb’s songs, including “Wichita Lineman”, “By the Time I Get to Phoenix” and “MacArthur Park”, have continued to find new audiences. He says Nick Cave and Flea have recorded “Wichita Lineman”, while the song’s reach has also been renewed through recent performances and recordings by other artists.

segments.title: Songs left in the drawer
segments.body: Webb’s new album, “Yours for the Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb”, gathers previously unheard songs, including material first intended for Dolly Parton and Frank Sinatra. He recalls Sinatra gently telling him that “Winter Clothes” was not quite finished; Webb says he finally returned to it years later.

content.headline: Sam Fender says high ticket prices for his stadium tour will be changed
content.shortHeadline: Sam Fender promises changes to stadium ticket prices
content.standfirst: After fans highlighted standing tickets listed at more than £130 for his 2027 tour, Fender said he was unhappy with the prices and promised the tiered standing arrangement would not go ahead.

image.caption: Sam Fender, who said he was unhappy with the tour’s ticket prices.

sources.originalTitle: Sam Fender tells fans high ticket prices for Proper Massive tour are ‘getting changed’

segments.body: Sam Fender has promised to change ticket prices for his 2027 stadium tour after fans criticised the cost of tickets advertised for Wembley. Standing tickets were listed at £98.85 and £130.75, with seats ranging from £64.75 to £130.75.

Fender said the prices had risen more than he intended and that they should reflect the cost of putting on the show. He also called the division between front and back standing areas “bollocks”, saying it would not happen on his tour. Tickets were due to go on sale on Friday, with a presale on Wednesday.

content.headline: James Dean Bradfield reflects on Manic Street Preachers’ ‘The Holy Bible’
content.shortHeadline: Manic Street Preachers face the weight of ‘The Holy Bible’
content.standfirst: The band’s new live release revisits the album whose lyrics were shaped by Richey Edwards. Bradfield describes the strain of performing it, the group’s response to Edwards’ disappearance and the limits of closure.

image.caption: Manic Street Preachers: Nicky Wire, James Dean Bradfield and Sean Moore.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: Manic Street Preachers have released “The Holy Bible Live”, recorded during a 2014 performance of their 1994 album in full. Frontman James Dean Bradfield recalls the anniversary concerts as a physical and emotional challenge: some lyrics, he says, weighed heavily on stage, while the band wanted to perform as a three-piece to evoke the group’s former line-up.

segments.title: Living with an absence
segments.body: Lyricist Richey Edwards disappeared in 1995 and is presumed to have died by suicide. Looking back on his bandmate’s mental health struggles, Bradfield says they were young and “just weren’t equipped to deal with it”, even though they tried to help. He rejects the idea that grief necessarily brings closure, while saying he is proud the band managed to connect with the album again.

content.headline: A Taylor Swift fan remembers discovering her on Myspace in 2006
content.shortHeadline: Before Taylor Swift was famous, fans found her on Myspace
content.standfirst: On the 20th anniversary of Swift’s debut album, a former teenage fan recalls the online community that formed around her early songs—and how an outsider’s discovery became a global phenomenon.

image.caption: Taylor Swift as a teenage country singer.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on Myspace in 2006

segments.body: Before Taylor Swift became a global star, the writer and a friend found her music through Myspace, where Swift shared details of her life and career. The essay recalls how teenagers exchanged comments, collected press clippings and made listening to a new country singer feel like belonging to a private club.

segments.title: A changing relationship with fame
segments.body: Swift’s self-titled debut, released in October 2006, offered songs about teenage relationships that made a strong connection with young listeners. Looking back, the writer sees both the closeness of Swift’s early online presence and the distance created by her subsequent fame, while reflecting on the way she helped make female songwriting and fan participation more visible.

content.headline: Heavensouls turns digital overload into intimate, shifting sound on ‘cantu of th
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls makes a restless collage feel intimate
content.standfirst: On “cantu of the sower”, producer Chidi Obialo combines free-jazz movement, electronic fragments and live instrumentation in a restless collage that the review hears as both disorienting and emotionally searching.

sources.originalTitle: cantu of the sower EP

segments.body: The 20-year-old producer heavensouls, also known as Chidi Obialo, builds “cantu of the sower” from shifting layers of percussion, strings, saxophone, samples and small electronic sounds. The review describes the album-length EP as a “collage of collages”, with pieces that move between apparent chaos and moments of calm.

The review connects the music’s density to Obialo’s movement between Nigeria, the US and online musical communities, while noting his stated interest in the claustrophobia of suburban life. Its sounds can feel crowded, but the critic finds that the record’s collisions are shaped by a personal thread rather than overload for its own sake.

content.headline: Caroline Rose finds humour and unease in ‘Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman
content.shortHeadline: Caroline Rose’s new album makes room for oddballs
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s seventh album turns a long-delayed song into a noisy, funny set of portraits, with suburban unease and more sombre reflections beneath its restless surface.

sources.originalTitle: Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall

segments.body: Caroline Rose’s “Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall” brings the long-gestating “Yip Yip Yow” to the front of an album of distorted guitars, fast tempos and comic characters. The review hears a deliberate break from the melancholy of Rose’s previous record, while finding that the jokes often carry darker concerns.

Rose’s songs look at outsiders and people struggling at the edges of everyday life. The reviewer points to “Conversation with Shiv”, which revisits a friend caught in drug use and financial trouble, as evidence that the album’s humour and its more vulnerable moments coexist rather than cancel each other out.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s ‘Back to Black’ reissue adds demos but leaves its legacy intact
content.shortHeadline: ‘Back to Black’ reissue adds detail, not a new story
content.standfirst: The 20th-anniversary edition includes a handful of unheard recordings, demos and a live set. The review celebrates Winehouse’s album while arguing that the extra material cannot fill the gap left by her lost work.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Amy Winehouse’s “Back to Black” remains the centrepiece of a 20th-anniversary set that adds early versions of songs, B-sides and a live recording from Amsterdam. The review finds the demos illuminating, particularly for showing how the album’s sound developed, and again praises Winehouse’s voice and the record’s mix of vintage influences with contemporary songwriting.

segments.title: What an archive cannot restore
segments.body: The new material is limited, and the review notes that the recordings Winehouse made for a planned follow-up were destroyed. The set offers useful glimpses into her work, but the critic argues that no anniversary package can replace the music that was never released.

content.headline: ‘Animol’ director Ashley Walters on prison, sobriety and breaking a cycle
content.shortHeadline: Ashley Walters turns hard-won experience into ‘Animol’
content.standfirst: After a career shaped by music, prison and acclaimed acting roles, Walters has directed his first feature. He discusses sobriety, masculinity and the memories that informed its young-offender setting.

image.caption: Ashley Walters, director of “Animol”.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life around

segments.body: Ashley Walters has directed “Animol”, a drama set in a young offenders’ institution. He says the film is not autobiographical, but drew on memories of his own time in prison. Its story follows teenagers navigating fear and violence, while also making room for tenderness and a queer romantic relationship.

segments.title: A different idea of masculinity
segments.body: Walters reflects on his own struggles with addiction and says he has been sober since entering rehabilitation in 2020. He sees a connection between “Animol” and “Adolescence” in their attention to young people and to the ways restrictive ideas about masculinity discourage men from talking about vulnerability.

content.headline: ‘All About the Money’ finds a wealthy heir and a commune’s unresolved tensions
content.shortHeadline: A commune, an heir and a film that leaves questions open
content.standfirst: Sinéad O’Shea’s documentary follows James “Fergie” Chambers, a multimillionaire who bankrolled a rural Massachusetts commune. The review finds a vivid, complicated subject, but says the film’s attempt at balance leaves its story unsettled.

image.caption: James “Fergie” Chambers in “All About the Money”.

sources.originalTitle: All About the Money review – confusion and compelling weirdness of wealthy leftwing heir

segments.body: James “Fergie” Chambers, an heir to a multimillion-dollar fortune, helped fund a small communist community in rural Massachusetts. After some members were arrested following a protest at an Israeli-owned arms manufacturer, the documentary follows the fallout among Chambers and former members, including Paige Belanger, while Chambers is abroad.

segments.title: An uneasy portrait
segments.body: The review praises filmmaker Sinéad O’Shea’s effort not to take sides, but says the result can feel muddled and leaves basic questions about the subject and the commune unresolved. Chambers is also facing a US extradition request from Spain over alleged support for Hamas; the review presents him as a compelling, troubled figure without resolving the allegations.

content.headline: Ashley Walters, Cyndi Lauper and more on why ‘That Thing You Do!’ endures
content.shortHeadline: Why “That Thing You Do!” still feels like a feelgood film
content.standfirst: A writer revisits Tom Hanks’s 1996 music comedy, finding joy in its fictional band’s sudden success and warmth in its refusal to pretend that creative lives always end happily.

image.caption: The fictional band the Wonders in “That Thing You Do!”.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movie

segments.body: Tom Hanks wrote, directed and starred in “That Thing You Do!”, the story of a fictional 1960s pop group whose fortunes change when a new drummer speeds up its song. The essayist recalls the thrill of the band hearing its music on the radio, and the film’s affection for the excitement of making something together.

segments.title: Hope without a perfect ending
segments.body: The film’s success is short-lived: relationships and competing ambitions pull the band apart. For the writer, that wistfulness is part of its appeal. The story offers the pleasure of vicarious success without hiding the trade-offs, and ultimately suggests choosing happiness over fame.

content.headline: ‘Never After Dark’ review: a Japanese ghost story with old-school charm
content.shortHeadline: A ghostbuster meets her match in “Never After Dark”
content.standfirst: Moeka Hoshi plays a travelling exorcist hired to investigate a haunting in Dave Boyle’s Japanese-language horror film, which the review finds charming and inventive even when its scares are familiar.

image.caption: Moeka Hoshi in “Never After Dark”.

sources.originalTitle: Never After Dark review – ghostbuster-for-hire meets her match in Japanese exorcism horror

segments.body: In “Never After Dark”, Moeka Hoshi plays Airi, a travelling ghostbuster whose dead sister appears to her in mirrors. A new job at a former hotel brings her into contact with a spirit whose damaged face hints at a more difficult haunting than she expected.

The review praises the film’s physical effects and its inventive use of reflections, wire work and a phenakistoscope in the exorcism scenes. It finds the scares somewhat predictable, but says Hoshi brings intelligence and spontaneity to a film that is otherwise a low-stakes, playful horror story.

content.headline: ‘Ever Since I Knew Myself’ examines childhood and conformity in Georgia
content.shortHeadline: A filmmaker revisits childhood and Georgia’s classrooms
content.standfirst: Maka Gogaladze’s debut documentary pairs conversations with her mother with observations of children’s lessons, examining strict education and the pressure to conform in Georgia.

image.caption: A classroom scene in “Ever Since I Knew Myself”.

sources.originalTitle: Ever Since I Knew Myself review – confronting the scars of childhood

segments.body: Maka Gogaladze opens her debut feature by recalling how, as an adolescent, she threw away her poems in an act of rebellion against her mother. She later puts her mother on camera to discuss demanding piano lessons and examinations that continued to trouble her into adulthood.

segments.title: Beyond one family
segments.body: The film also observes children in history, ballet, dance and art classes, where the review sees an emphasis on discipline and little room for individual expression. It says the shifts between personal memories and these wider scenes can feel abrupt, but points to the film’s interest in how national identity and collectivism shape education.

content.headline: ‘The Social Reckoning’ turns Facebook’s harms into a personal warning
content.shortHeadline: “The Social Reckoning” looks at Facebook’s impact—and ours
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network” dramatises reporting on Facebook’s internal research. The writer found it frightening, but questions how readily viewers can separate their own lives from the company’s influence.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning”.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: “The Social Reckoning” centres on Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen, whose disclosures exposed internal research into the platform’s effects, including its impact on teenage girls and the promotion of extremist groups. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in the film, written and directed by Aaron Sorkin.

segments.title: The harder question
segments.body: The review describes the film as a tense investigation that makes social media’s influence feel close to home. But its writer returns to scrolling after watching, acknowledging a dependence on Meta’s services for work and social connection. The film’s warning, the essay argues, matters in part because many people feel unable simply to leave.

content.headline: Why women are falling for the basket-made husband in “Wicker”
content.shortHeadline: The unlikely appeal of “Wicker”’s basket-made husband
content.standfirst: The film’s unusual romance—about a woman who commissions a basketmaker to weave her a husband—has sparked online fascination. Its creators and commentators connect the appeal to domestic labour, desire and outsiderhood.

sources.originalTitle: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In “Wicker”, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who asks a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to make her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård plays the resulting wicker man. The trailer and a suggestive promotional popcorn bucket helped prompt a wave of online jokes and fan enthusiasm.

segments.title: A fantasy with a domestic edge
segments.body: Filmmakers Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson say the character’s attentiveness is part of the appeal: he notices work that needs doing without expecting praise. Writer Gillian Daniels and academic Indira Neill Hoch place the film among monster romances that explore desire, difference and what audiences consider attractive or threatening.

content.headline: Elizabeth Holmes remains a mystery in the documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
content.shortHeadline: A new documentary returns to Elizabeth Holmes’s story
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim follow Holmes before she reports to prison, letting her defend herself without resolving the central question: whether her claims of innocence reflect conviction or manipulation.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes, the subject of “You Can See Everything”.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster

segments.body: “You Can See Everything” follows Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted Theranos founder, in the period before she reported to prison. In interviews and observed scenes with her family, Holmes insists that she did not lie and that her company’s blood-testing device worked, claims set against her conviction for defrauding investors.

segments.title: Questions without a verdict
segments.body: The film’s directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, do not settle how to interpret Holmes. A later conversation adds a voice that questions both her account and Fielder’s response to it. The feature says the documentary’s mix of comedy and unease leaves viewers with competing possibilities rather than a definitive conclusion.

content.headline: “This City Is Ours” returns with its Liverpool gangland drama intact
content.shortHeadline: “This City Is Ours” returns to Liverpool’s criminal world
content.standfirst: The second series brings back the Phelan crime family and its complicated loyalties. The review praises the performances and tension, as well as the small domestic details that keep the drama grounded.

image.caption: James Nelson-Joyce as Michael in “This City Is Ours”.

sources.originalTitle: This City Is Ours review – the Liverpudlian gang drama is back … and the acting’s as terrific as ever

segments.body: The second series of “This City Is Ours” opens with Michael trying to leave the Phelan crime family behind, only to be drawn into a new crisis involving the family of a rival cartel boss. The review praises the ensemble, including Shaun Evans as newcomer Ozzie Thompson, and singles out a tense car-wash sequence.

The series’ appeal, the review argues, lies partly in its unglamorous details: characters worry about IVF, family obligations and everyday chores alongside murder and drug deals. These mundane touches make the drama’s misguided, often violent characters feel more human—and more compelling—than slicker crime-series archetypes.

content.headline: Bill Murray’s Irish golf travelogue struggles to find its way
content.shortHeadline: Bill Murray’s Irish golf show looks like a trip gone wrong
content.standfirst: The review of “A Course Called Ireland” finds strained encounters, awkward narration and long, silent car journeys, with only occasional glimpses of Murray’s charm or reflections on his Irish heritage.

image.caption: Bill Murray in “A Course Called Ireland”.

sources.originalTitle: A Course Called Ireland review – why did Bill Murray ever agree to this Irish golf show?

segments.body: In “A Course Called Ireland”, Bill Murray travels around Ireland playing golf and reflecting on his family history. The review describes a series that appears unsure whether it is about golf, Murray or the Irish, and criticises its decision to use a local woman, Margaret, as an inexperienced narrator.

Murray is often reluctant to follow the production’s prompts, the review says, leaving quiet car journeys and strained conversations that the show tries to cover with forced quirkiness. There are brief moments when he is thoughtful about his Irish ancestry or charming with locals, but they do not rescue the travelogue for the critic.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from “Nocturne” to Matthew Perry’s story
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream, including a Matthew Perry documentary
content.standfirst: This week’s recommendations range from a prison-set thriller starring Stephen Graham to an intimate series about Matthew Perry, alongside a low-key comedy and a darts contest.

image.caption: Stephen Graham in the thriller “Nocturne”.

sources.originalTitle: Nocturne to The One About Matthew Perry: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Guardian’s weekly guide picks seven programmes to stream. Among them is “Nocturne”, a claustrophobic thriller in which Stephen Graham plays a serial killer in a prison psychiatric ward, and a three-part documentary about Matthew Perry, combining interviews with friends and family with an account of his rise and struggles.

The selection also includes “Minimum Wage”, a mockumentary about teenagers running a struggling pizzeria, and a Netflix darts competition featuring amateurs facing champion Luke Littler. The guide describes the latter as a short-format contest where an upset could bring a share of a £501,000 prize.

content.headline: “Escaping Idi Amin” brings Asian Ugandans’ expulsion into view
content.shortHeadline: Ugandan Asians recall Idi Amin’s expulsion order
content.standfirst: A two-part documentary hears from people who were children when Idi Amin ordered Uganda’s Asian population to leave in 90 days, recording memories of violence, fear and displacement.

image.caption: A military officer in “Escaping Idi Amin”.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Idi Amin’s forced expulsion of Asians from Uganda

segments.body: In 1972, Idi Amin gave Uganda’s Asian population 90 days to leave the country. “Escaping Idi Amin” hears from people who experienced the expulsion as children, including accounts of curfews, daily radio countdowns, street violence and massacres.

The programme is a two-part documentary, with the first episode scheduled for BBC Two. The television guide describes its testimonies as complex as well as frightening, bringing personal recollections of the expulsion to the centre of the history.

content.headline: “One Born Every Minute” returns with an intimate account of childbirth
content.shortHeadline: “One Born Every Minute” returns to the delivery room
content.standfirst: The reviewer welcomes the birth series’ return after eight years, arguing that its close attention to three women’s experiences makes visible a major life event often left out of public conversation.

image.caption: Faye with her first baby in “One Born Every Minute”.

sources.originalTitle: One Born Every Minute is back – and it’s wild, essential TV

segments.body: Channel 4’s “One Born Every Minute” returns after an eight-year break, following three women through very different births: a first baby after previous miscarriages, a planned caesarean after a traumatic birth and a later pregnancy. The reviewer, drawing on her own experience of childbirth, calls the episode tense and life-affirming.

segments.title: Making private experience visible
segments.body: The essay argues that birth is often treated as too intimate to discuss, despite its physical and emotional intensity. By showing the women’s experiences and the roles of their partners and medical staff, the programme offers a shared public space for stories that might otherwise be quickly set aside.

content.headline: “Gone Fishing” gives Ted one last trip with Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse
content.shortHeadline: “Gone Fishing” says goodbye to its beloved dog Ted
content.standfirst: The series’ new opener includes a final, posthumous fishing trip for Ted, the much-loved dog who became an unofficial third member of the cast. The review reflects on the show’s warmth and its candid approach to ageing.

image.caption: Ted, the much-loved dog from “Gone Fishing”.

sources.originalTitle: Goodbye Ted, the grumpy canine heart of Gone Fishing

segments.body: A special episode of “Mortimer and Whitehouse: Gone Fishing” brings Ted back for one final trip on the River Ribble. The Patterdale terrier, adopted by executive producer Lisa Clark, died in April. The review recalls how his grumbling persona and comic moments made him a much-loved presence in the series.

segments.title: A show about friendship and time
segments.body: The review notes that the programme has always paired humour with frank conversations about health and ageing. Ted’s absence makes that perspective more poignant, but the writer says the show’s appreciation of nature, friendship and the present keeps the tribute from becoming simply sad.

content.headline: Prince William’s “Graham Norton” appearance was a carefully judged PR move
content.shortHeadline: What Prince William gained from the “Graham Norton” sofa
content.standfirst: The writer sees the prince’s relaxed, full-hour appearance as an effective demonstration of approachability, linking it to Kensington Palace’s effort to shape his public image.

image.caption: Prince William on “The Graham Norton Show”.

sources.originalTitle: The real reason Prince William appeared on Graham Norton

segments.body: Prince William appeared on “The Graham Norton Show” alongside Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin, promoting his Earthshot Prize. The essay says he stayed for the full programme, joked with the host and spoke about his interests, creating a more relaxed impression than a brief promotional appearance would have done.

segments.title: A public image at work
segments.body: The writer argues that the appearance fitted an effort to present William as an “average millennial dad” and a forward-looking figure. Comparing it with Prince Harry’s more personal interview, the essay sees the contrast as favourable to William, while acknowledging that the monarchy’s publicity operation is part of the picture.

content.headline: Miranda Hart’s exit from “The Celebrity Traitors” becomes a moment of joy
content.shortHeadline: Miranda Hart brought warmth to “The Celebrity Traitors”
content.standfirst: An essay celebrates Hart’s humour and vulnerability on the reality series, noting that her return to television after years of illness made her exit especially affecting.

image.caption: Miranda Hart in “The Celebrity Traitors”.

sources.originalTitle: Miranda has brought wholesome joy back to TV

segments.body: After seven episodes, Miranda Hart was murdered in “The Celebrity Traitors”. The essay recalls her comic highlights, from the accidental moustache in a challenge to teaching a dance move that inspired the imaginary group “Big Mix”, and says her warmth made her a standout presence.

segments.title: Laughter and connection
segments.body: Hart has spoken about struggling with chronic fatigue syndrome and being largely bed-bound for years. After her exit, she described how meaningful it had been to reconnect with laughter, work and other people. The essay argues that her willingness to show vulnerability helped make the moment moving amid the show’s games and backstabbing.

content.headline: Lara Croft’s 30-year career has had its share of missteps
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft at 30: the low points as well as the icons
content.standfirst: A look back at “Tomb Raider” highlights the rushed sequels, awkward spin-offs and marketing choices that often misunderstood Lara Croft—even as she remained one of gaming’s defining characters.

image.caption: Lara Croft in “Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered”.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: Thirty years after Lara Croft’s debut, the retrospective recalls how “Tomb Raider” became a hit and made its heroine a gaming icon. It also revisits the series’ less successful moments, including annualised releases that wore down developer Core Design and the poorly received “Tomb Raider: Chronicles”.

segments.title: An icon repeatedly misread
segments.body: The article criticises later games and marketing for leaning on Lara’s sexualised image or placing her in stories that diminished her agency. Its broader case is that her lasting appeal comes from being a capable, enigmatic adventurer—and that developers and marketers repeatedly missed what players valued about her.

content.headline: “Penguin Colony” turns an Antarctic expedition into an unsettling adventure
content.shortHeadline: A penguin explores “Penguin Colony”’s strange Antarctica
content.standfirst: This unusual exploration game sends players waddling through an Antarctic landscape shaped by Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and fragments of language. Its rough edges do not diminish its ambition, the review argues.

image.caption: A penguin in “Penguin Colony”.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: In “Penguin Colony”, players explore Antarctica as a penguin, moving between ice fields, ruins and increasingly strange landscapes. The game draws on H P Lovecraft’s “At the Mountains of Madness”, but reframes the expedition’s human arrogance through a small bird collecting words rather than treasure.

segments.title: A world built from contradictions
segments.body: The review praises the game’s unsettling combination of low-poly exploration, historical material and a narrator’s account of an earlier expedition. It notes occasional audio and control problems, but says the ending challenges both Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi brutality, and invites players to explore without human-style urgency.

content.headline: Ubisoft Paris moves from Mario to tactical combat with “Rainbow Six Tactics”
content.shortHeadline: How Ubisoft Paris changed gears for “Rainbow Six Tactics”
content.standfirst: The studio behind “Mario + Rabbids” is making a turn-based “Rainbow Six” spin-off. Its developers explain how planning, player choice and realistic settings shape the shift.

image.caption: A scene from “Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics”.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Ubisoft Paris is moving from “Mario + Rabbids” to “Rainbow Six Tactics”, a turn-based spin-off of “Rainbow Six Siege”. The preview describes a mission in Nigeria in which a squad uses drones, explosives and coordinated movement to enter a guarded warehouse.

segments.title: Planning and player choice
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says the series’ emphasis on preparation and consequential decisions suits a tactics game. He wants players to experiment rather than follow one prescribed route, while level designer Julien Vial describes the challenge of making locations feel realistic compared with the studio’s more fantastical Mario environments.

content.headline: A father and son replay the first game they played together
content.shortHeadline: Replaying “Modern Warfare 2” brings a father and son together
content.standfirst: A father revisits co-op missions from his son’s childhood, finding that better teamwork—and the time they share—matters more than finally completing the game.

image.caption: A scene from “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2”.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2”, the first game they played together when the son was five. Older now, they try again at co-op missions they never completed, including one known to them as “the guard dogs in the snow”.

segments.title: More than a high score
segments.body: Their different play styles initially get them into trouble, but they learn to divide the work and communicate. The writer sees the sessions as a rare chance to play without everyday pressures, and as a meaningful period of closeness before father and son move to different parts of the world.

content.headline: New footage renews scrutiny of infant monkey experiments at US lab
content.shortHeadline: Footage renews scrutiny of infant monkey research
content.standfirst: Video released by Peta shows infant macaques in experiments at the University of Washington that ended in 2020. The university says the work contributed to public-health research; the footage has reopened questions about animal welfare and the value of the findings.

image.caption: A still from footage released by Peta showing infant macaque research at the University of Washington.

sources.originalTitle: Peta releases video showing experiments on infant monkeys at University of Washington

segments.body: Footage released by animal-rights group Peta shows newborn macaques separated from their mothers and undergoing neurological tests at the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center. The experiments, which ran from 2014 to 2020, investigated possible effects of prenatal exposure to domoic acid, a toxin produced by marine algae.

segments.title: What the research established
segments.body: Records cited in the report say researchers administered domoic acid to 32 pregnant macaques and removed 28 infants from their mothers after birth. The university says the studies contributed to understanding how prenatal exposure may affect learning and memory. The report says there is no clear evidence the work changed public-health recommendations.

segments.title: Welfare questions remain
segments.body: Peta and primate-welfare experts criticise separating the infants from their mothers. The university says maternal relationships and early development are important welfare considerations and that experienced staff cared for the animals. It says there are no current infant studies at the centre, though protocols for such studies remain active.

content.headline: Phone photos help researchers track changing shorelines across 21 countries
content.shortHeadline: Phone photos track changing shorelines
content.standfirst: CoastSnap turns repeat photographs taken by the public into a record of beach change. Researchers use the images to study erosion, storm impacts and whether beach replenishment schemes are working.

image.caption: Praa Sands beach in Cornwall, where a CoastSnap station helps researchers monitor shoreline change.

sources.originalTitle: How citizen science is tracking changes in shorelines around the world

segments.body: CoastSnap invites people to place a phone in a fixed cradle at a beach and send in a photograph. Because the camera position stays roughly the same, software can align images taken over time, map the shoreline and adjust for the tide using each photo’s timestamp.

Researchers use the resulting records to follow longer-term coastal erosion, examine the effects of individual storms and monitor beach replenishment. The project, which began in Australia in 2017, now has more than 200 stations in 21 countries and is described as the largest coordinated land-based coastal monitoring programme in the world.

content.headline: Data centre boom pits local communities against AI infrastructure plans
content.shortHeadline: The data centre boom meets local resistance
content.standfirst: Residents are challenging the noise, land use and potential pollution of new data centres, while companies warn that opposition could delay construction. The debate is over who benefits from the infrastructure—and who bears its costs.

image.caption: Protesters oppose a data centre in North Ayrshire.

sources.originalTitle: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened

segments.body: The rapid expansion of data centres built to support cloud services and AI is bringing conflict to communities near proposed and operating sites. In Newport, residents describe losing light and facing persistent noise from a growing campus; in Cardiff, a proposed facility on a hospital park-and-ride site has drawn more than 1,200 planning objections. The BBC counts about 12,250 data centres worldwide, up from roughly 8,000 operational sites in 2021.

segments.title: Power has an environmental cost
segments.body: A Houston Advanced Research Center analysis modelled possible pollution from Texas data centres over five years.
